chapters.title: One public address
chapters.text: Visitors send event requests to one endpoint. The load balancer selects an application target so visitors do not need to know individual server addresses.

chapters.title: Share requests
chapters.text: Alternate requests between App A and App B. This shares turns, but a slow request can still occupy one target much longer than another.

chapters.title: A target fails
chapters.text: App A stops passing readiness checks. Detection takes time; requests already in flight may fail and must be handled safely by the client.

chapters.title: Use the healthy target
chapters.text: New requests go to App B after the target is removed. App B needs enough spare capacity; routing cannot manufacture capacity during an outage.

chapters.title: Protect the booking
chapters.text: Both copies use the same order system. A repeated booking request carries the same idempotency key so a lost response does not charge twice.

chapters.title: Measure the whole path
chapters.text: Check latency and errors at the balancer, application and database. If both applications wait on the database, adding routing rules will not fix that bottleneck.

chapters.title: Observe demand
chapters.text: The application serves visitors while metrics record utilization and request behavior. Select a signal related to the constrained resource, not simply the easiest chart.

chapters.title: Choose a target
chapters.text: The controller compares the observed signal with a configured target and computes a desired replica count within minimum and maximum limits.

chapters.title: Request capacity
chapters.text: The controller requests more replicas. Scheduling, image download, initialization and health checks take time. Desired capacity and ready capacity can differ.

chapters.title: Wait for readiness
chapters.text: Only ready replicas should receive normal traffic. If nodes or quotas are exhausted, a controller cannot create the missing physical capacity by itself.

chapters.title: Check dependencies
chapters.text: More application copies can increase database connections. Limit aggregate concurrency so solving an application bottleneck does not create a database outage.

chapters.title: Scale down carefully
chapters.text: After demand falls, stabilization prevents rapid shrinking and regrowth. Drain work before removing replicas and keep enough minimum capacity for the next burst.

chapters.title: Define success
chapters.text: For this example, success means a correct booking response within its latency objective. A homepage response alone does not measure the same user outcome.

chapters.title: Spread the copies
chapters.text: Applications run in separate zones behind a resilient entry point. The goal is to avoid losing every application copy to the same local failure.

chapters.title: Lose one zone
chapters.text: Zone A becomes unavailable. Detection and rerouting consume time, and requests already in flight may fail. The objective allows an explicitly measured error budget.

chapters.title: Use remaining capacity
chapters.text: Zone B receives new work. It must have enough capacity, network access and working credentials to serve the actual user operation.

chapters.title: Follow the data
chapters.text: Both application copies need a suitable data service. A single unprotected database can still interrupt bookings even when both application zones are healthy.

chapters.title: Test the objective
chapters.text: Run a controlled failure and measure booking success and recovery time. Availability is demonstrated by user outcomes, not by counting boxes in a diagram.

chapters.title: Separate essential work
chapters.text: The event page needs correct booking information, but recommendations are optional. Give these paths different deadlines and resource budgets.

chapters.title: An optional call stalls
chapters.text: Recommendations stop responding. Without a boundary, waiting calls can consume all connections or workers and affect otherwise healthy operations.

chapters.title: Enforce a deadline
chapters.text: The timeout guard ends waiting for optional work. This protects local resources but does not prove a remote write was cancelled or never happened.

chapters.title: Degrade honestly
chapters.text: Render the essential page without suggestions. Do not turn an uncertain payment outcome into a success message just to make the page appear healthy.

chapters.title: Bound retries
chapters.text: If a retry is appropriate, limit attempts and use backoff with jitter. Preserve one operation identity for side effects so retries do not create duplicate business actions.

chapters.title: Test partial failure
chapters.text: Inject a slow response and a lost reply in a safe test environment. Verify core capacity and user-visible correctness rather than only testing a clean server shutdown.

chapters.title: Start with one copy
chapters.text: One application serves event pages. Its safe measured capacity is finite, and a restart can interrupt every request reaching that copy.

chapters.title: Add another copy
chapters.text: Deploy the same application on another machine or process. Horizontal scaling adds peers rather than increasing resources inside the original machine.

chapters.title: Share incoming work
chapters.text: Routing sends requests to ready replicas. Balance according to workload characteristics; more boxes are useful only when requests can reach them.

chapters.title: Move durable state
chapters.text: Both replicas use the same appropriate storage for files, sessions or records. A file written only to Replica A will not magically appear on Replica B.

chapters.title: Find serial work
chapters.text: If every request waits on one locked database operation, extra applications may add waiting instead of throughput. Trace and load-test the complete path.

chapters.title: Test the gain
chapters.text: Compare throughput and tail latency before and after scaling. Also remove one replica to check that remaining copies serve users correctly with available capacity.

chapters.title: Measure the wait
chapters.text: The application is slow. Inspect whether requests wait on CPU, memory, storage, locks or another service before selecting a bigger machine.

chapters.title: Increase resources
chapters.text: Give the same database more appropriate resources. This is vertical scaling because the number of independent database copies has not increased.

chapters.title: Watch useful memory
chapters.text: More memory can hold more of the hot working set. If disk reads were the bottleneck, the experiment may show lower latency.

chapters.title: Plan interruption
chapters.text: A size change may restart or fail over the database. Use the actual platform procedure and verify what users see during the transition.

chapters.title: Retest the result
chapters.text: Repeat the same controlled workload. Compare throughput, tail latency, waits and cost; do not use machine size as the success metric.

chapters.title: Keep a recovery plan
chapters.text: The larger machine still needs redundancy and backups. If the machine fails or reaches its size ceiling, a different design decision is needed.

chapters.title: Request a description
chapters.text: The reader asks for a public event description. The key identifies the resource and representation; private results need appropriate identity scoping.

chapters.title: Serve a hit
chapters.text: A reusable cached value returns quickly. Its age matters: a fast response can still be too stale for the business operation.

chapters.title: Handle a miss
chapters.text: If the value is absent or expired, fetch from the source of truth. A miss is normal and must have bounded latency and safe error handling.

chapters.title: Control refill work
chapters.text: Many readers may miss the same hot key together. Coalesce loads or bound refill work so the cache does not amplify pressure on the database.

chapters.title: Store a temporary copy
chapters.text: Populate the cache with an explicit lifetime. Plan what happens after an update and whether serving an older value is acceptable during refresh.

chapters.title: Test a cold cache
chapters.text: Remove the cache in a safe test. Observe source traffic, latency and errors. A warm hit-rate chart alone does not prove the architecture can recover.

chapters.title: Choose the route
chapters.text: A visitor requests a public poster. The content delivery network routes the request to a suitable edge location rather than always going directly to the origin.

chapters.title: Return a cached asset
chapters.text: If the edge has a valid copy, it returns that representation. This can reduce both response latency and repeated origin transfer.

chapters.title: Fetch on a miss
chapters.text: A missing or expired representation needs an origin fetch. The origin and its network path still matter for uncached work.

chapters.title: Use a versioned URL
chapters.text: When asset bytes change, publish a new content-versioned name. Long-lived immutable caching only fits a URL whose content will not change.

chapters.title: Separate private data
chapters.text: An account or booking response may be personal and time-sensitive. Do not place it on the shared public cache path without a deliberately safe policy.

chapters.title: Measure each path
chapters.text: Compare edge hits, misses and private requests separately. A fast cached poster does not show whether the booking API meets its latency and correctness objectives.

chapters.title: Enter one API boundary
chapters.text: The client calls a public API address. The gateway provides a shared routing boundary instead of requiring clients to know every internal service location.

chapters.title: Apply coarse policy
chapters.text: Validate the request and supported identity credentials with maintained security libraries. Reject oversized or invalid traffic before forwarding expensive work.

chapters.title: Route by responsibility
chapters.text: Event requests go to the event service; order requests go to the order service. API versions and paths should have deliberate routing rules.

chapters.title: Authorize the record
chapters.text: The order service checks ownership and allowed actions using verified identity. Passing gateway authentication does not grant access to another visitor order.

chapters.title: Bound aggregation
chapters.text: If one API request fans out, set deadlines and partial-failure behavior. A slow optional service should not hold every gateway worker indefinitely.

chapters.title: Operate the entry tier
chapters.text: Trace requests through the boundary and test gateway capacity and redundancy. Centralizing policy is useful, but it also creates an important operational dependency.

chapters.title: Identify the principal
chapters.text: Requests are assigned a deliberate identity key, such as a verified account and endpoint. A spoofable header cannot safely define a protected client budget.

chapters.title: Refill the budget
chapters.text: The token bucket refills over elapsed time up to its capacity. Capacity permits a bounded burst while the refill rate controls sustained use.

chapters.title: Consume atomically
chapters.text: Checking and consuming a token must behave as one operation for shared state. Separate reads and writes can overspend under concurrency.

chapters.title: Allow affordable work
chapters.text: A request with enough tokens proceeds, but still faces authorization, request validation and downstream concurrency limits. Passing the limiter is not a correctness guarantee.

chapters.title: Reject excess traffic
chapters.text: A request without budget receives a clear rejection and retry guidance where appropriate. Clients should wait rather than creating an immediate retry storm.

chapters.title: Plan storage failure
chapters.text: If the shared limiter fails, enforce the chosen endpoint policy and alert. Independent local counters do not preserve a strict global quota across replicas.

chapters.title: Closed: calls flow
chapters.text: The breaker allows normal calls and records eligible outcomes. Timeouts still bound each attempt; a closed breaker is not a guarantee of health.

chapters.title: Observe repeated failures
chapters.text: The dependency times out repeatedly. A minimum sample and measurement window help distinguish a pattern from a single unlucky request.

chapters.title: Open: stop pressure
chapters.text: The breaker opens and rejects dependency calls quickly. This frees local resources and avoids repeating expensive failures while recovery is investigated.

chapters.title: Choose an honest fallback
chapters.text: Optional recommendations can be omitted. Essential payment outcomes must remain pending or failed according to verified state, not invented to hide the outage.

chapters.title: Half-open: probe
chapters.text: After a reset interval, allow a limited probe set. Sending every waiting caller at once can overload a dependency that is only partly recovered.

chapters.title: Recover or reopen
chapters.text: Successful probes restore normal traffic; failed probes reopen the breaker. Observe both false trips and recovery behavior under controlled failure tests.

chapters.title: Record outgoing work
chapters.text: A booking succeeds and records a receipt job reliably. Coordinate this with business storage, for example using an outbox, so a crash does not lose the obligation.

chapters.title: Buffer a burst
chapters.text: The queue stores work while consumers catch up. Stored backlog buys time, but retention, storage and acceptable delay remain finite.

chapters.title: Process within limits
chapters.text: Workers pull jobs at a safe rate. Their combined concurrency must respect email provider quotas and other downstream capacity.

chapters.title: A worker crashes
chapters.text: A worker can send an email and fail before acknowledging its job. The queue may deliver that same logical job again.

chapters.title: Protect the effect
chapters.text: Use stable job identity and an appropriate idempotency or reconciliation strategy. A delivery guarantee alone does not guarantee exactly one external effect.

chapters.title: Handle persistent failure
chapters.text: After bounded attempts, move a poison job to a monitored dead-letter path. Investigate and repair before controlled replay instead of retrying forever.

chapters.title: Commit a business fact
chapters.text: The booking owner establishes that the booking is confirmed, then reliably publishes the associated fact. Publication and storage must have an explicit failure strategy.

chapters.title: Fan out independently
chapters.text: The event channel makes the fact available to separate subscribers. Each subscriber has a distinct business responsibility and its own processing state.

chapters.title: One subscriber lags
chapters.text: Analytics becomes slow while receipt processing continues. Subscriber delay is observable; it should not silently redefine the original booking outcome.

chapters.title: Deliver the event twice
chapters.text: A repeated delivery uses the same logical event identity. Consumers must avoid awarding points or producing another external effect accidentally.

chapters.title: Evolve the contract
chapters.text: Add compatible fields carefully and test old consumers. Retained events and delayed subscribers may outlive the latest deployment.

chapters.title: Plan recovery and replay
chapters.text: Replay analytics when appropriate, but do not resend historical receipts automatically. Reprocessing policy depends on the side effects owned by each subscriber.

chapters.title: Write at the owner
chapters.text: A booking write reaches the current primary. Its acknowledgment policy determines what the application can assume about durability and replication at that moment.

chapters.title: Ship changes
chapters.text: Changes travel to replicas. With asynchronous replication, the primary can reply before all copies have applied the latest write.

chapters.title: Read a lagging copy
chapters.text: A confirmation read reaches Replica A before the booking arrives there. The user may see an older state even though the primary accepted the write.

chapters.title: Choose a consistent path
chapters.text: Use the primary or an explicitly supported consistency mechanism for confirmation. Public catalog reads can have a different staleness allowance.

chapters.title: Coordinate failover
chapters.text: If the primary fails, promotion needs a clear election or orchestration process and fencing. Avoid letting an isolated old writer accept conflicting new changes.

chapters.title: Keep recovery separate
chapters.text: Replication also copies many mistakes. Maintain tested backups and recovery points independently rather than counting live copies as protection against every kind of data loss.

chapters.title: Identify the record home
chapters.text: A request carries a tenant or entity key. The routing rule maps that key to an authoritative shard before data is read or written.

chapters.title: Distribute independent records
chapters.text: Different record groups live on different database shards. This can spread storage and write work when the groups are actually independent enough.

chapters.title: Find a hot key
chapters.text: One popular event can overload its shard even when every shard has the same row count. Workload distribution matters more than counting keys.

chapters.title: Examine a global query
chapters.text: A query across all events may contact every shard and merge results. Cross-shard joins, transactions and uniqueness require deliberate support or redesign.

chapters.title: Move ownership safely
chapters.text: Rebalancing needs copying, verification, a write/cutover policy and an updated routing map. Changing a modulo number does not move existing records.

chapters.title: Choose the simplest fit
chapters.text: Shard only when requirements and measurements justify the coordination cost. A suitable index or larger database may solve the current problem with much less complexity.

chapters.title: Define a partition rule
chapters.text: History rows are grouped by date. This organization can exist inside one database and should not be confused with distributing ownership across independent shards.

chapters.title: Create ranges
chapters.text: Each month has a defined range with explicit boundaries. Future data needs a matching partition or a deliberately configured default behavior.

chapters.title: Ask for November
chapters.text: A date-bounded query reaches the planner. The engine can eliminate irrelevant ranges if its rules and the query expression permit partition pruning.

chapters.title: Read the useful part
chapters.text: The November partition supplies the requested history. An appropriate index and query plan can still be necessary inside that partition.

chapters.title: Maintain the lifecycle
chapters.text: Retention can operate on old partitions, but removal is a data-policy decision. Verify dependencies, recovery requirements and correct boundaries before destructive maintenance.

chapters.title: Know the boundary
chapters.text: A query without the partition key may still inspect many parts. More partitions do not automatically add machines, guarantee speed or fix one hot-row lock.

chapters.title: Find the capabilities
chapters.text: Name business responsibilities before drawing services. Catalog descriptions and authoritative seat reservations have different ownership and correctness requirements.

chapters.title: Own the data
chapters.text: Each capability owns its protected state and exposes contracts. Giving every service write access to every table defeats much of the intended independence.

chapters.title: Cross a network boundary
chapters.text: The booking workflow contacts payments. That call can time out or succeed remotely while its response is lost; it is not a local transaction.

chapters.title: Decouple optional work
chapters.text: Confirmation can publish notification work after reliable business-state coordination. A slow email provider need not occupy the booking request indefinitely.

chapters.title: Deploy compatibly
chapters.text: Old and new callers may coexist. Test contract compatibility and observe version-specific errors instead of requiring every service to deploy in lockstep.

chapters.title: Justify the complexity
chapters.text: For a small team, a modular monolith may satisfy the same domain boundaries with fewer moving parts. Choose services from requirements rather than fashion.

chapters.title: Ask for a stable name
chapters.text: The caller requests the payment capability by service name instead of storing an individual pod address that may disappear during the next deployment.

chapters.title: Maintain endpoints
chapters.text: The platform or registry tracks service destinations and readiness. Registration and removal need reliable ownership and observable convergence.

chapters.title: Choose a destination
chapters.text: Client or server routing selects a usable endpoint. Discovery and load balancing cooperate, but they describe different responsibilities.

chapters.title: Replace an instance
chapters.text: An old instance becomes unready and a replacement joins. Cached addresses and existing connections can outlive the registry update.

chapters.title: Retry within a budget
chapters.text: A failed connection may use a safe bounded retry against current membership. Do not hide repeated errors with unlimited retries.

chapters.title: Verify service identity
chapters.text: Knowing an address does not authorize a request. Validate the relevant identity, transport security and resource permissions at the appropriate boundaries.

chapters.title: Receive the public request
chapters.text: The browser talks to one public address. The reverse proxy represents backend servers rather than acting as the browser own outbound proxy.

chapters.title: Apply forwarding rules
chapters.text: Host and path rules select a backend. Request size, deadlines, TLS termination and supported protocols must fit the actual workload.

chapters.title: Forward the request
chapters.text: API traffic reaches the API backend and asset traffic can reach another backend. A reverse proxy can also perform load-balancing duties.

chapters.title: Preserve trusted context
chapters.text: Forward useful request context, but do not accept forged identity or client-IP headers from arbitrary clients as trusted facts.

chapters.title: Handle streaming deliberately
chapters.text: Buffering and idle/read timeouts can change what a browser sees. Test streams and long-lived connections end to end instead of assuming default behavior fits.

chapters.title: Protect the proxy tier
chapters.text: The public entry point needs its own capacity, redundancy and monitoring. Backend replicas do not help if the only proxy is unavailable.

chapters.title: Look up the name
chapters.text: The browser or operating system asks a resolver for the hostname. Existing local or resolver caches may already contain an answer.

chapters.title: Query authority if needed
chapters.text: A resolver without a usable cached answer follows DNS resolution to the authoritative records. Record type and delegation must be configured correctly.

chapters.title: Use a cached answer
chapters.text: A client may connect to the old endpoint while its answer is still valid. Changing the authoritative record does not instantly erase that cached answer.

chapters.title: Fetch the new answer
chapters.text: Later lookups can obtain the new destination. Clients and resolvers change at different times, so old and new endpoints may both receive traffic.

chapters.title: Verify beyond DNS
chapters.text: The new address also needs the correct certificate, host routing and healthy application. Successful resolution alone does not prove the website works.

chapters.title: Plan safe overlap
chapters.text: Keep a rollback path and an appropriate overlap interval. Lower TTL in advance when useful; do not expect a last-second TTL edit to end existing connections.

chapters.title: Set recovery objectives
chapters.text: Define how long the required user operation may be unavailable and how much recent data loss is acceptable. These are explicit business objectives, not product defaults.

chapters.title: Preserve recoverable state
chapters.text: Capture suitable backups and change logs with recoverable keys and configuration. Live replication alone may copy deletion or corruption to every current replica.

chapters.title: Lose production
chapters.text: A serious failure interrupts the production environment. Recovery needs an environment, permissions and an executable runbook, not merely a promise that a backup exists.

chapters.title: Restore in isolation
chapters.text: Rebuild required infrastructure and restore data in a safe environment. Include secrets, certificates, queues and other dependencies required for actual user workflows.

chapters.title: Validate before routing
chapters.text: Query restored data and run correctness checks. A process reporting restore complete does not prove that bookings, ownership and payment reconciliation are usable.

chapters.title: Measure and improve
chapters.text: Restore traffic safely and compare measured end-to-end recovery and data loss with the objectives. Record gaps, improve the runbook and repeat the drill.

chapters.title: Serve the old version
chapters.text: Visitors use the existing version while the next release is prepared. Establish user-visible metrics and rollback conditions before shifting traffic.

chapters.title: Start the replacement
chapters.text: Create new capacity without immediately removing all old instances. Download, initialization and dependency setup take time and need spare resources.

chapters.title: Check readiness
chapters.text: The readiness gate verifies the instance can serve the intended request. A running process with missing dependencies should not receive normal traffic yet.

chapters.title: Shift traffic gradually
chapters.text: Send a bounded share to the new version and drain old work deliberately. Monitor errors and latency for real user operations, not only process health.

chapters.title: Keep data compatible
chapters.text: Both versions can access the database during rollout. Expand and migrate safely before removing fields or behavior the old version still needs.

chapters.title: Validate rollback
chapters.text: Stop or reverse traffic movement if the release violates its criteria. Code rollback cannot magically reverse incompatible or destructive data changes.

chapters.title: Start one operation
chapters.text: The gateway starts or receives trace context for checkout. Its span represents one part of the operation, not all system traffic.

chapters.title: Propagate context
chapters.text: Booking receives compatible context and creates a related span. Without propagation, downstream records can appear as unrelated operations.

chapters.title: Record parallel work
chapters.text: Database and payment calls run in parallel in this teaching example. Their intervals overlap, so adding both durations would overstate wall-clock time.

chapters.title: Collect span evidence
chapters.text: Instrumentation exports spans to an observability backend. Export buffering, sampling and failures mean a trace view is not a complete audit of every request.

chapters.title: Find the slow boundary
chapters.text: Compare the critical path, errors and dependency waits. Combine traces with aggregate metrics to determine whether the visible slow request reflects a widespread problem.

chapters.title: Protect telemetry data
chapters.text: Do not attach secrets or unnecessary personal data to spans. Keep attribute cardinality, access, sampling and retention within a deliberate observability budget.

chapters.title: Map required flows
chapters.text: The public client needs the web tier, which needs booking. Booking needs the database. Record required ports and dependencies before introducing isolation.

chapters.title: Remove unnecessary paths
chapters.text: The unrelated worker has no business requirement to contact the orders database. Blocking that path reduces reachability and potential blast radius.

chapters.title: Allow a narrow connection
chapters.text: Permit the actual booking workload to use the configured database port. Broad namespace-wide rules may allow more callers than intended.

chapters.title: Verify enforcement
chapters.text: A policy object is only configuration intent. The cluster network implementation must support and enforce it, and selectors must match the intended workloads.

chapters.title: Keep identity checks
chapters.text: An allowed TCP connection is not permission to read every order. Database credentials, encrypted transport and application ownership checks remain separate controls.

chapters.title: Test both directions
chapters.text: Verify allowed traffic, denied traffic and necessary DNS/monitoring dependencies. Observe unexpected failures and refine the policy without silently opening everything.

chapters.title: Define the regional goal
chapters.text: Decide whether another region is for disaster recovery, nearby reads or active writes. Each operation can have different latency, availability and consistency requirements.

chapters.title: Copy suitable state
chapters.text: Region A sends changes toward Region B. Asynchronous copying can lag; synchronous coordination adds waiting and depends on the communication path.

chapters.title: Lose the connection
chapters.text: The regions cannot communicate. Allowing both to confirm the same last seat independently can violate correctness even though both applications are running.

chapters.title: Fence and promote
chapters.text: A safe failover establishes which writer owns new decisions and prevents the old writer from conflicting. Routing alone does not settle database ownership.

chapters.title: Route and validate
chapters.text: Direct eligible traffic to the recovery region and validate the actual booking workflow. Its capacity, credentials and dependencies must work independently enough for the failure scenario.

chapters.title: Plan reconciliation and failback
chapters.text: After recovery, reconcile lag and in-flight work before moving ownership back. Test both failover and failback instead of treating the first traffic switch as the whole plan.
